Daniel’s proposal is a vivid restatement of *inquiry/discovery learning*—the idea (associated with [Jerome Bruner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Bruner) and broader [constructivist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructivism_(philosophy_of_education)) pedagogy) that students understand more deeply when they reconstruct concepts rather than merely receive them. The hidden assumption is that “coming up with” a model is a reasonably well-defined, comparable act across domains; but the examples range from *discoverable from constraints* (midpoint with compass-and-straightedge) to *social conventions* (MLA) where “inventing” is the wrong verb, because what matters is legibility, interoperability, and institutional adoption. A student could devise a perfectly coherent citation scheme and still fail the real-world function of MLA—which is not elegance but coordination—so the program needs to distinguish *derivation of ideas* from *buy-in to standards*.

The grading rule—“percentage of models you come up with”—also risks rewarding performative novelty over justified understanding. Once the metric is “invent something,” you invite cheap reinventions and superficial variations, and you penalize the central academic skill of *using* existing models well and knowing when they apply. A more robust version of Daniel’s vision would grade (1) the quality of the reconstructed argument (clarity of assumptions, internal consistency, and evidence), (2) the ability to connect one’s reconstruction to the canonical form (“Here is how my limit definition matches the standard ε–δ definition; here is what it buys and what it costs”), and (3) epistemic humility: recognizing when a field’s “models” are not timeless truths but evolving, contested tools. In other words, the goal shouldn’t be to constantly reinvent the wheel; it should be to learn why the wheel is round, when it fails, and how people agreed on its standard size.
